A prefix sum array turns a running total into data you can query instead of recomputing: P[i] is the sum of the first i elements, with P[0] defined as 0, the sum of no elements, the empty prefix. Building it once costs O(n); after that, the sum of any range from a start up to, but not including, an end is one subtraction, P(end) minus P(start), because the difference cancels out everything the two prefixes share.

The shape of problem that signals it is many range-sum queries over data that doesn't change, or a subarray question phrased as "sum equals k", "divisible by m" or "as many of one kind as another". The technique's second use turns that question about a range into one about two single prefixes: a subarray from s up to e sums to k precisely when P(e) minus P(s) equals k, which is Two Sum restated over prefixes. Unlike a sliding window, it works with negative numbers, because it looks up one exact value instead of deciding whether a running sum should grow or shrink.

The mechanism is a hash map built alongside the running prefix, in one pass: for each new prefix, look up the value it would need a partner at, using what the map already holds, and only then record the prefix you have now computed. The map stores either how many times a prefix value has occurred, to count subarrays, or the earliest index it occurred at, to find the longest run. It has to start already holding the empty prefix, because a subarray that begins at index 0 has no earlier prefix to subtract.

The mistake that shows up under pressure is leaving that seed out: every subarray starting at index 0 goes uncounted, and the bug shows only on inputs where such a subarray exists, so a light test can miss it. The other is recording a prefix before looking it up, which can match an empty subarray against itself, and, once negative numbers are involved, trusting C++'s
, whose sign follows the dividend, so two prefixes in the same remainder class get different keys unless folded back into range.

You meet this in the interview question itself: after O(n) setup, answer any range-sum query in O(1), or turn "how many subarrays sum to k" into a hash-map lookup over running prefixes, seeded with the one representing nothing yet.

A prefix array answers range sums on data that doesn't change. Each change to one element moves every prefix after it, so updates cost O(n). When updates and queries mix, a Fenwick tree gives O(log n) for both; for this topic the data stays fixed.

The second idea turns a question about subarrays into a question about pairs of prefixes. Write P(i) for the sum of the first i elements. A subarray from index s up to, but not including, e sums to k exactly when P(e) − P(s) = k, that is, when P(s) = P(e) − k. So "how many subarrays sum to k" becomes "for each end e, how many earlier prefixes equal P(e) − k". That is the Two Sum question over prefix sums, and it has the same three steps as in the hash map topic. Decide what the map stores: a prefix value, with either how often it has appeared, to count subarrays, or the first index where it appeared, to find the longest. For each new prefix P(e), look up P(e) − k among the prefixes already recorded. Then record P(e).

The map starts with the empty prefix already in it: value 0, seen once, at index 0. Without it, every subarray that starts at index 0 is missed, because its matching prefix, the empty one, was never recorded. This is the commonest bug with the technique, and the edges section shows it.

This works with negative numbers, where a sliding window doesn't. A window has to decide whether to shrink by looking at its sum, and that needs sums that grow as the window grows. The map never makes that decision: it looks up one exact value. The whole run is one pass, O(n) time on average and O(n) space for the map.

The same idea works with other operations. With multiplication, the empty prefix is 1, the product of no elements, and the product of the elements after index i is a suffix product. The second exercise uses both. With XOR, the prefix of the first i elements lets you find subarrays whose XOR is k, because XOR undoes itself: P(e) XOR P(s) is the XOR of the elements between them.

To recognise a prefix-sum problem, look for sums over contiguous ranges asked many times, or "subarray sum equals k", "divisible by m" or "balanced" (as many of one kind as of another), especially when the numbers can be negative.
